title: Weighted Scheduling
explain: Weighted scheduling shares capacity in proportion to weights instead of always favouring one class. Strict priority says tier 1 first, always; weighted scheduling says tier 1 gets 70 percent and tier 2 gets 30, so nobody starves while important classes still get more. Random weighted choice gives the ratio only on average; round robin variants give a hard bound.
model:
Setup: several queues, each with a weight (the user's example: Tier 1 70 percent, Tier 2 30 percent).

| Variant | How | Guarantee |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Weighted random** | Pick queue by probability | Ratio on average only; 0.7^20 is about 0.08 percent chance of 20 straight misses, which happens often at thousands of picks per second |
| **Weighted round robin** | Each cycle: tier 1 seven times, tier 2 three times (smooth WRR interleaves) | Hard bound on the gap between turns |
| **Deficit round robin** | Each queue gets a quantum of credit per round, spends it by task cost, carries remainder | Fair by **cost**, not task count |

Rules:

- **Work-conserving:** if the chosen queue is empty, serve another; shares are computed over non-empty queues (5:3:2 with the middle empty gives 5/7 and 2/7).
- **Cost matters:** a 70/30 split by count with 0.1 s tasks vs 1 s tasks gives the 30 percent queue about 81 percent of worker time. Use DRR.
- Combine: **strict for an emergency class, weighted for the rest.**

Compare [strict priority](#/sd/f/prioritized-scheduling); the policy usually lives in the [dispatcher](#/sd/f/dispatcher).

details.q: Weights 5:3:2, the middle queue is empty, scheduler is work-conserving. What share goes to the first queue while the others are backlogged?
details.a: 5/7, about 71.4 percent, and 2/7 (28.6 percent) to the third. Weights are renormalised over the non-empty queues.

details.q: Two queues are served 70:30 by count; A tasks cost 0.1 s, B tasks cost 1.0 s. What share of worker time does B get?
details.a: In 100 dispatches A uses 70 x 0.1 = 7 s and B 30 x 1.0 = 30 s, so B gets 30/37, about 81 percent, despite its 30 percent weight. Weighting by count is only fair when costs are similar; deficit round robin charges by cost.

details.q: A product manager wants a guarantee that a queue-2 task never waits more than 10 dispatches under 70/30 random choice. Can you promise it?
details.a: No. Random choice gives the ratio only on average; the chance of 10 straight misses is 0.7^10, about 2.8 percent. For a bound use deterministic WRR or DRR, or reserved slots.

details.q: Free and premium tenants share workers, and a platform-incident class must pre-empt everything. Which combination?
details.a: Strict priority for the incident class, plus weighted shares (say 80/20) between premium and free. Premium gets more, free always progresses, incidents always win.

details.q: Walk through one round of deficit round robin.
details.a: Visit a queue and add its quantum to its deficit counter; while the head task's cost fits in the deficit, dispatch it and subtract the cost; if the queue empties, reset its deficit to zero; move on. Unused credit carries to the next round.

Weighted for steady-state fairness among tenants or tiers where every class must make progress. Strict (with limits) for emergency traffic that must always win. See [prioritized scheduling](#/sd/f/prioritized-scheduling) for the failure modes strict brings.

prompts.q: Compare weighted random, weighted round robin and deficit round robin.
points: Random: right ratio only on average, no bound on a single wait
DRR: credit spent by task cost

prompts.q: Design the scheduling policy for premium, free and incident traffic.
points: Weighted shares between premium and free
Premium gets more but free never starves

prompts.q: Explain why weighting by task count can be unfair and how to fix it.
points: A queue with expensive tasks consumes most worker time
Example: 70/30 count with 0.1 s vs 1 s gives about 81 percent time to the 30 queue
Charge by cost with deficit round robin
